Work from the project root, the main folder of the course. Read each step before you run its R chunk. All data are simulated. These exercises cannot show a finding about a real disease.

The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the course words. Each module reads its input files from disk. You do not need a saved R workspace.

```{r knit_setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
setwd(start_dir)
```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
```

## Module 1 at a glance {#module-1-overview}

**What you will do.** You will look at the files that come out of a genotyping laboratory. You will read a table of array sites, a laboratory report and a sample sheet. You will then check the size of the genotype files that the rest of the course uses.

**What you will learn.**

- What a SNP, an allele and a genotype are, and how they differ.
- How a genotyping array turns fluorescent light into a genotype call.
- What the Global Screening Array measures, and what it cannot measure.
- Why one row in a laboratory file is not always one person.
- Which laboratory problems the quality-control steps of later modules will look for.
- How data sources differ, and what the common file formats contain.
- Why large projects share different formats for different tasks.

**How long it takes.** About 90 minutes. Steps 1.8 to 1.11 are reading only. You can pause after 1.7 and return to the format examples later.

## 1.1 SNPs and genotypes {#step-1-1}

### What we do

Learn the difference between a DNA site, an allele and a genotype.

### Why

A [variant](../docs/glossary.md#variant) is a position in the DNA where people differ. An [allele](../docs/glossary.md#allele) is one of the possible DNA letters at that position. A [single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)](../docs/glossary.md#snp) is a variant where one single DNA base changes.

At an ordinary [autosomal](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) site, a person carries two copies, one from each parent. A site with the alleles A and G can therefore give three [genotypes](../docs/glossary.md#genotype): A/A, A/G or G/G. A missing value is not a fourth allele. The X, Y and mitochondrial chromosomes need different rules for the number of copies. We discuss them at step 4.5.

### You need

The checked array annotation file from step 0.5. An [annotation](../docs/glossary.md#annotation) is a table that describes each site on the array.

### Command

```{r s1-1}
ann <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "array", "sim2026_array_annotation.tsv"))
cat(nrow(ann), "rows in the annotation\n")
head(ann[c("Name", "Chr", "Position_GRCh38", "Ref_Plus", "Alt_Plus")])
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

A table with the site name, the chromosome, the [GRCh38](../docs/glossary.md#grch38) position and the two alleles on the [plus strand](../docs/glossary.md#plus-strand). GRCh38 is the version of the human reference genome that gives the positions. The annotation contains 299,523 rows. Array site names are not always rs identifiers.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

At a C/T autosomal site, does C/T represent two variants or one genotype?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

One genotype at one variant. The person carries one C allele and one T allele.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.2 How an array measures DNA {#step-1-2}

### What we do

Learn why a fluorescence measurement is not the same as a genotype call.

### Why

A genotyping [array](../docs/glossary.md#genotyping-array) is a small chip that measures many sites at once. It measures fluorescent light from DNA that sticks to [probes](../docs/glossary.md#probe). This sticking is called hybridisation. Probes are short DNA sequences that are designed to recognise chosen sites.

The chip reads the light in two colour channels. The signals from many samples tend to form three [clusters](../docs/glossary.md#intensity-cluster) of points. The clusters stand for the two [homozygotes](../docs/glossary.md#homozygote) (two equal alleles) and the [heterozygote](../docs/glossary.md#heterozygosity) (two different alleles). A calling algorithm then gives each sample a genotype, or leaves the call missing.

The signal strength is a measurement. It is not a count of alleles. Weak separation between clusters, background light and mixed DNA can make a call uncertain.

### You need

The array annotation from step 1.1. You also need the example final reports supplied at step 0.5. A [final report](../docs/glossary.md#final-report) is a text file from the laboratory that lists the genotype calls.

### Command

```{r s1-2}
reports <- list.files(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "final_report"), full.names = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(reports) == 3L)
readLines(reports[1], n = 12L)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The top of a simulated Final Report: first the header, then the start of the data section. The supplied reports contain genotype calls and GC scores. They do not contain raw intensity data, so you cannot redraw cluster plots in this exercise.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Can a low-quality fluorescence measurement be treated as a confidently observed missing allele?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Missing means that no genotype call was accepted. It is not a biological allele.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.3 The Global Screening Array {#step-1-3}

### What we do

Learn what the array measures and what it leaves unmeasured.

### Why

The Illumina Global Screening Array (GSA) measures a chosen set of sites. It is not [whole-genome sequencing](../docs/glossary.md#whole-genome-sequencing), which reads almost every base. If a site is not on the array, we know nothing about it. We cannot say that the variant is absent.

The simulated course data use GSA-style Illumina site names and real GRCh38 positions. The manufacturer manifest is not shared with students. A manifest is the full design file of the array. The annotation for students has only the fields that this course needs. It does not copy the full proprietary design.

### You need

The annotation that you inspected at step 1.1.

### Command

```{r s1-3}
table(ann$Chr)
stopifnot(nrow(ann) == 299523L, !anyDuplicated(ann$Name))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Autosomes 1 to 22, plus X, Y and MT (mitochondrial DNA). There are 299,523 array entries at the start. The same genomic site can appear under two different names. We review this at step 4.5.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

If a site is absent from the array, can you conclude that every participant has the reference allele there?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. If a site is absent from the array, it was not measured directly.

</details>

## 1.4 From sample to scanned chip {#step-1-4}

### What we do

Follow the identity of a sample through a plate and a laboratory well.

### Why

Several laboratory steps come before the export. The laboratory extracts the DNA, checks its concentration, copies it, cuts it into pieces, hybridises it to the chip, stains it and scans it.

A [plate](../docs/glossary.md#plate-and-well) is a tray that holds laboratory wells processed together. A well is one small hole in the tray that holds one sample. A well can contain a [technical replicate](../docs/glossary.md#technical-replicate), which is a second measurement of the same person. So one row in a laboratory file is not always one unique person.

A [batch effect](../docs/glossary.md#batch-effect) is a systematic difference caused by how samples were processed, for example by a faulty plate. It is not caused by the [phenotype](../docs/glossary.md#phenotype), the trait that we study.

### You need

The sample sheet from step 0.5. The [sample sheet](../docs/glossary.md#sample-sheet) lists every well with its plate, its sample name and any replicate label.

### Command

```{r s1-4}
sheet <- read.csv(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "lab_export", "sample_sheet.csv"), colClasses = "character")
table(sheet$Plate)
sum(nzchar(sheet$Replicate_of))
stopifnot(nrow(sheet) == 2016L)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Twenty-one plates, each with 96 wells, give 2,016 measurements. Sixteen wells are labelled as technical replicates. The simulation started from 2,000 people.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

A plate has 96 wells and two are replicates of other wells. Must it contain 96 different people?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. A well is one measurement. A person is one biological individual.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.5 Calling genotypes {#step-1-5}

### What we do

Read the call and score columns, and do not treat the score as certainty.

### Why

The calling algorithm compares the measured intensities with the expected clusters. The [GC score](../docs/glossary.md#gc-score) measures the quality of one call. It is not the probability that an association is true. It is not a [p-value](../docs/glossary.md#p-value) either.

A [no-call](../docs/glossary.md#no-call) is a site where the algorithm gave no genotype. It can come from a weak signal or from unclear clusters.

The example files use semicolons between columns and decimal points in numbers. This is on purpose. A character that separates columns is called a [delimiter](../docs/glossary.md#delimiter). Check the delimiter in the file. Do not change the language of your computer.

### You need

The example final reports from step 1.2.

### Command

```{r s1-5}
lines <- readLines(reports[1], warn = FALSE)
start <- match("[Data]", lines)
example <- read.table(text = lines[(start + 1L):length(lines)], sep = ";", header = TRUE, quote = "", check.names = FALSE, colClasses = "character")
head(example)
summary(as.numeric(example[["GC Score"]]))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The columns are SNP Name, Sample ID, GC Score, Allele1 - Plus and Allele2 - Plus. The examples are short excerpts of reports. They are not the full table of 299,523 sites for every person.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does GC Score = 0.9 mean a variant has a 90% chance of causing disease?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The score describes the quality of the genotype call. It says nothing about disease or association.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.6 Problems born in the laboratory {#step-1-6}

### What we do

Link laboratory problems to the quality-control checks of later modules.

### Why

Little DNA in a well can cause many no-calls. Contamination, which means a mix with foreign DNA, can increase the number of heterozygous calls. A sample swap can make the recorded sex differ from the sex seen in the genotypes. It can also create duplicate samples with conflicting information.

A processing batch can affect many samples together. One pattern alone does not prove its cause. Keep the logs and ask the laboratory to confirm before you change any sample identity.

[QC](../docs/glossary.md#qc) means quality control. It is a set of checks that remove avoidable errors before the statistical tests.

### You need

The sample sheet and the score examples from steps 1.4 and 1.5.

### Command

```{r s1-6}
stopifnot(all(c("Plate", "Well", "Sample_ID", "Replicate_of") %in% names(sheet)))
head(sheet)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The table has the information that you need to study batch membership and labelled replicates. No person is removed in module 1.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

If many samples from one plate have low call rates, what shared cause should you investigate before attributing the pattern to disease?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A processing or batch problem. A plate pattern suggests a shared laboratory cause, but it does not prove one.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.7 The export {#step-1-7}

### What we do

Understand how the reports relate to the genotype files used for the analysis.

### Why

The report excerpts show how calls are labelled. The complete genotype table for the course is stored in a matching [BED/BIM/FAM set](../docs/glossary.md#bed-bim-fam). The BED file stores the genotypes in a compact binary form. The BIM file describes the variants. The FAM file describes the samples and their order.

These three files belong together as one set. In module 2 we convert them to the native PLINK 2 format, called PGEN/PVAR/PSAM. We check the sample identity and order during the conversion.

### You need

The matched laboratory export from step 0.5, and the ideas from steps 1.1 to 1.6.

### Command

```{r s1-7}
initial <- check_bed(cfg$input)
print(initial)
stopifnot(initial$samples == 2016L, initial$variants == 299523L)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

2,016 sample wells and 299,523 variants. No QC has been applied yet. The first FAM file has no case/control phenotype.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows with the supplied simulated dataset.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Can you combine a BED from one release with a FAM from another if their sample counts match?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Equal counts do not prove that the sample identity, the order or the genotypes match.

</details>

## 1.8 Where genetic data come from {#step-1-8}

Reading, about 5 minutes. You can come back to it later.

### What we do

Compare ways to measure genetic variation. This course uses simulated array data.

### Why

A [read](../docs/glossary.md#read) is a sequence measured from one DNA molecule. [Sequencing](../docs/glossary.md#sequencing) reads bases. An [array](../docs/glossary.md#genotyping-array) measures signals at selected sites instead. [Depth](../docs/glossary.md#sequencing-depth) counts reads covering a base. [Density](../docs/glossary.md#marker-density) counts tested sites across a region. These are different quantities.

A [targeted panel](../docs/glossary.md#targeted-panel) tests selected genes or regions. An [amplicon](../docs/glossary.md#amplicon) is a DNA segment copied before sequencing. The [exome](../docs/glossary.md#exome) is the protein-coding part of the genome. [Imputation](../docs/glossary.md#imputation) predicts unmeasured alleles using a reference group. [Summary statistics](../docs/glossary.md#summary-statistics) report group-level results instead of individual genotypes.

Costs below are relative for large research studies. They depend on sample numbers, preparation and analysis. They are not price quotes. A typical depth is a study design choice, not a guarantee for every base.

| Source | What is measured | Density or depth | Strength | Blind spot | Relative cost and typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Illumina Infinium Global Screening Array (GSA) and Global Diversity Array (GDA) | Fluorescence at selected SNPs | Hundreds of thousands to a few million sites, depending on design | Many samples at low cost | Most unselected and rare sites are not directly measured | Low; common-variant association |
| Thermo Fisher Axiom arrays | Probe signals at selected sites | Hundreds of thousands of sites or more, depending on design | Large studies and custom content; UK Biobank used Axiom | Content and calling quality depend on design | Low; population studies |
| Targeted panels and amplicons | Reads from chosen regions | Often hundreds of reads per target base | Detailed measurements in selected genes | Regions outside the panel are absent; copying can bias [allele balance](../docs/glossary.md#allele-balance) | Low to medium; focused research or clinical testing |
| Whole-exome sequencing | Reads from [captured](../docs/glossary.md#sequence-capture) coding regions | Often tens to over 100 reads per target base | Many rare coding variants | Most non-coding regions and some difficult exons are missed | Medium; coding-variant studies |
| [Short-read](../docs/glossary.md#short-read) [whole-genome sequencing](../docs/glossary.md#whole-genome-sequencing) | Reads across the genome | About 30x is a common research design | Broad measurement of common and rare variation | Repeats and [large rearrangements](../docs/glossary.md#structural-variant) can remain difficult | High; discovery across the genome |
| [Low-pass](../docs/glossary.md#low-pass) whole-genome sequencing plus imputation | Sparse reads followed by predicted genotypes | Often below a few reads per base | Broad coverage at lower sequencing cost | Rare alleles and poorly represented ancestries can be harder to predict | Low to medium; large cohorts with a suitable reference |
| Newer sequencing platforms: Roche SBX, Element AVITI, MGI/Complete Genomics DNBSEQ and Ultima | DNA sequence from whole genomes or selected regions | Genome-wide or target coverage; depth is selected for the study | Fast turnaround or high sample throughput, depending on the platform | Error patterns and difficult regions need platform-specific checks | Platform and batch dependent; large-scale sequencing |
| Oxford Nanopore (ONT) long reads | Electrical signals converted to long sequences | Depth varies; reads can span many thousands of bases | Repeats, large rearrangements, long-range context and [native base modifications](../docs/glossary.md#base-modification) such as [5mC](../docs/glossary.md#5mc) | DNA quality, errors and analysis choices matter | Medium to high; complex variation |
| PacBio high-fidelity (HiFi) long reads | Repeated observations combined into accurate long sequences | Depth varies; reads often span many thousands of bases | Accurate long reads, complex variation and [native base modifications](../docs/glossary.md#base-modification) such as [5mC](../docs/glossary.md#5mc) | Preparation, DNA quality and cost constrain designs | Medium to high; genome discovery |
| Imputed genotypes | Probabilities inferred from measured data and a reference | Often millions of predicted variants | Wider coverage without measuring every site | Predictions are uncertain and reference-dependent | Low added analysis cost; association at untyped sites |
| Summary statistics | Effects and uncertainty from an association analysis | One row per tested variant | Share results without sharing individual calls | Cannot recover each person's genotype or redo every model | Low storage cost; combining studies |

Roche sequencing by expansion (SBX) is a single-molecule, [nanopore-based](../docs/glossary.md#nanopore) method: it reads a molecule through a tiny sensor opening. It is designed for speed. Roche describes reads up to about 1,500 bases with suitable sample preparation. [Roche SBX](https://diagnostics.roche.com/us/en/news-listing/2026/axelios-1-next-generation-sequencing-platform.html), [Element AVITI](https://docs.elembio.io/docs/tools/software-tools/), [MGI/Complete Genomics DNBSEQ](https://www.completegenomics.com/products/sequencing-platforms/dnbseq-t7-plus/) and [Ultima](https://www.ultimagenomics.com/products/analysis-and-bioinformatics/) all feed workflows using standard formats. These include [FASTQ](../docs/glossary.md#fastq) for reads and qualities, [BAM/CRAM](../docs/glossary.md#sam-bam-cram) for read records, and [VCF](../docs/glossary.md#vcf-bcf) for variants. Alignment matches reads to a reference. Variant calling assigns alleles from the evidence.

Native [base modifications](../docs/glossary.md#base-modification) are chemical changes present on the original DNA. [Methylation](../docs/glossary.md#methylation) adds a small chemical group. [5mC](../docs/glossary.md#5mc) means 5-methylcytosine, a modified C base. [ONT](https://nanoporetech.com/support/software/data-analysis/can-i-detect-modified-bases) and [PacBio HiFi](https://www.pacb.com/products-and-services/applications/epigenetics/) can detect it from native DNA with suitable analysis models. This adds information beyond the A, C, G and T sequence.

**Official documentation:** [Illumina GSA](https://www.illumina.com/products/by-type/microarray-kits/infinium-global-screening.html), [GDA](https://www.illumina.com/products/by-type/microarray-kits/infinium-global-diversity.html), [Thermo Fisher arrays](https://www.thermofisher.com/us/en/home/life-science/microarray-analysis.html), [Roche SBX outputs](https://diagnostics.roche.com/gb/en/diagnostics-insights/sbx-data-analysis-resources.html), [ONT output specifications](https://nanoporetech.github.io/ont-output-specifications/26.01/read_formats/pod5/) and [PacBio HiFi](https://www.pacb.com/technology/hifi-sequencing/).

**References:** [Infinium, PMID 15838508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15838508/); [Axiom, PMID 21565264](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21565264/); [HiFi, PMID 31406327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31406327/); [UK Biobank, PMID 30305743](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30305743/).

### You need

The array explanation at 1.2. No extra dataset is needed.

### Command

No code to run. This is a reading-only step.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

You can distinguish a measured array call, a sequence read and an imputed prediction. This course starts from array calls.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Do not compare array density with sequencing depth. They measure different things. Follow the glossary links before reading the table again.

</details>

### Quick check

Would deeper sequencing of a small panel reveal variants everywhere in the genome?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. More depth improves measurements inside the targets. It does not add regions outside them.

</details>

### Files created

None.

## 1.9 A map of genetic file formats {#step-1-9}

Reading, about 6 minutes. You can come back to it later.

### What we do

Follow the files from an instrument to an association result.

### Why

A [file format](../docs/glossary.md#file-format) defines how information is stored. A [text file](../docs/glossary.md#text-binary) contains readable characters. A binary file encodes records as bytes. A [pipeline](../docs/glossary.md#pipeline) is a sequence of processing steps. Different instruments can reach the same analysis format.

**[IDAT](../docs/glossary.md#idat)** stores Illumina array fluorescence and scanner information. It precedes genotype calling.

**[BPM/CSV manifest](../docs/glossary.md#array-manifest)** describes array probes and sites. BPM is binary; CSV is text with values separated by commas.

**[EGT cluster file](../docs/glossary.md#egt)** stores Illumina calling [clusters](../docs/glossary.md#intensity-cluster), the signal groups used to assign genotypes. It is not a sample genotype matrix.

**[GTC](../docs/glossary.md#gtc)** stores a sample's Illumina genotype calls and related measurements. It is a binary output of calling software. [DRAGEN Array converts GTC to VCF](https://help.dragenarray.illumina.com/overview/our-features).

**[Final Report](../docs/glossary.md#final-report)** is a configurable Illumina text export. Rows usually describe sample-marker measurements; the selected columns must be checked.

**[CEL](../docs/glossary.md#cel)** stores probe intensities from Thermo Fisher/Affymetrix arrays. It needs the matching array definitions and calling software. [Axiom analysis software](https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/GSD/brochures/axiom-analysis-suite-user-guide.pdf) exports PLINK, VCF or text for later analysis.

**[BCL](../docs/glossary.md#bcl)** stores Illumina sequencing base calls and quality information by instrument cycle. Sample separation produces read files for downstream analysis.

**[FASTQ](../docs/glossary.md#fastq)** stores each read's identifier, sequence and base-quality characters. It does not normally say where the read belongs in the genome.

**[POD5 and FAST5](../docs/glossary.md#pod5-fast5)** store Oxford Nanopore raw signals and [metadata](../docs/glossary.md#metadata), the information describing a measurement. POD5 replaces legacy FAST5. [Basecalling](../docs/glossary.md#basecalling) translates signals into sequence reads.

**[SAM/BAM/CRAM](../docs/glossary.md#sam-bam-cram)** store reads and their [alignments](../docs/glossary.md#alignment), the proposed matches to a reference. Sequence Alignment/Map (SAM) is text. Binary Alignment/Map (BAM) is compressed binary. BAM can also hold reads before alignment. An [unaligned BAM (uBAM)](../docs/glossary.md#ubam) stores read sequences and qualities without genomic placements. [PacBio HiFi reads are delivered in unaligned BAM](https://pacbiofileformats.readthedocs.io/en/12.0/BAM.html). [ONT Dorado writes BAM by default](https://software-docs.nanoporetech.com/dorado/1.2.0/); without an alignment step, those reads are unaligned. CRAM compresses read information, often using a matching reference. BAI/CSI and CRAI are [indexes](../docs/glossary.md#index), small companion files that help retrieve a region.

**[gVCF](../docs/glossary.md#gvcf)** means genomic Variant Call Format. It is a VCF convention for one sample's variant evidence and reference blocks. A reference block describes a stretch represented as non-variant. It is not simply a list of variant sites.

**[VCF/BCF](../docs/glossary.md#vcf-bcf)** store variants, alleles and sample fields. Variant Call Format (VCF) is text. Its binary counterpart is BCF. [bgzip](../docs/glossary.md#bgzip-tabix) compresses data in independently readable blocks. Tabix indexes sorted genomic text, including compressed VCF; TBI or CSI is the companion index.

**[Hail MatrixTable and VariantDataset](../docs/glossary.md#hail-formats)** are directory-based stores for large analyses. MatrixTable separates variant rows, sample columns and entry values. VariantDataset keeps variant data and reference blocks separately to avoid expanding every reference call.

**[BGEN](../docs/glossary.md#bgen)** stores genotypes or [genotype probabilities](../docs/glossary.md#genotype-probability), the probabilities of possible calls, in a compact binary format. A separate `.sample` file can describe samples; some BGEN files also embed identifiers. A [`.bgi` index](https://biobank.ctsu.ox.ac.uk/showcase/label.cgi?id=100319) supports fast lookup of variants in the matching BGEN file.

**[GEN](../docs/glossary.md#gen)** is a text probability format. It usually gives three probabilities per sample for each two-allele site, plus variant and allele fields.

**[PED/MAP](../docs/glossary.md#ped-map)** is an older PLINK text pair. PED has one row per sample with allele pairs; MAP lists variants in the same order.

**[TPED/TFAM](../docs/glossary.md#tped-tfam)** is the transposed PLINK text pair. TPED has one row per variant; TFAM gives the sample order.

**[BED/BIM/FAM](../docs/glossary.md#bed-bim-fam)** is the older PLINK binary genotype set. BED stores calls, BIM variants and FAM samples. It is unrelated to UCSC BED.

**[PGEN/PVAR/PSAM](../docs/glossary.md#pgen-pvar-psam)** is the PLINK 2 native set. PGEN stores calls and can also store dosages; PVAR describes variants and PSAM describes samples.

**[UCSC BED](../docs/glossary.md#ucsc-bed)** is a text format for genomic intervals. Its start is zero-based and its end is excluded.

**[GFA](../docs/glossary.md#gfa)** describes sequence graphs. Segments and links can represent alternative paths through a genome.

**[FASTA/FAI](../docs/glossary.md#fasta-fai)** stores named sequences and their byte index. A [contig](../docs/glossary.md#contig) is a continuous sequence, such as our invented `toy1`.

**[GWAS-SSF](../docs/glossary.md#gwas-ssf)** standardises association summary statistics for sharing. It requires defined columns and study metadata, not just a renamed table.

| Format group | Typical producer | Text or binary | Content | Pipeline position |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IDAT; BPM/CSV; EGT; GTC; Final Report | Illumina scanner and array software | Binary, except CSV and Final Report | Signals; probe definitions; clusters; calls; exported table | Array measurement to called genotypes |
| CEL | Thermo Fisher array software | Binary in common current uses; older text variants exist | Probe intensities | Before array calling |
| BCL | Illumina sequencer software | Binary | Cycle-level calls and qualities | Before read export |
| FASTQ; unaligned BAM (uBAM) | Basecaller, sample separation software, PacBio HiFi or ONT Dorado | FASTQ text; uBAM binary | Reads, qualities and optional read annotations | Before alignment |
| POD5; FAST5 | ONT instrument software | Binary | Raw signals and read metadata | Before basecalling |
| SAM; BAM; CRAM; BAI/CSI/CRAI | Basecalling or alignment software and SAMtools | SAM text; others binary | Reads, optional alignments and region indexes | Before or after alignment, then variant calling |
| gVCF; VCF; BCF; TBI/CSI | Variant callers, BCFtools and imputation tools | VCF/gVCF text; BCF and indexes binary | Reference blocks, variants, calls or probabilities | Calling to analysis |
| MatrixTable; VariantDataset | Hail | Binary directory stores | Distributed variant, sample and entry data | Large-scale processing |
| BGEN; BGI; GEN; sample | Imputation and conversion software | BGEN/BGI binary; GEN/sample text | Probabilities, variant index and sample descriptions | Imputation to association |
| PED/MAP; TPED/TFAM | PLINK | Text | Calls and identities | Older analysis exchange |
| BED/BIM/FAM | PLINK | BED binary; BIM/FAM text | Calls and identities | Compact called-genotype analysis |
| PGEN/PVAR/PSAM | PLINK 2 | PGEN binary; PVAR/PSAM text, optionally compressed | Calls, dosages and identities | Current PLINK analysis |
| UCSC BED | Annotation software | Text | Half-open intervals | Region annotation |
| GFA | Genome assembly software | Text | Sequence graph segments and links | Assembly and complex variation |
| FASTA/FAI | Reference providers and SAMtools | Text | Sequences and byte offsets | Reference input |
| GWAS-SSF | Association tools plus a formatter | Text, usually compressed | Effects, uncertainty and study metadata | Result sharing |

**Four checks apply across formats.** A [genome build](../docs/glossary.md#genome-build) names the reference version. A file extension does not prove its build. [Coordinates](../docs/glossary.md#coordinate-system) may count from zero or one. VCF position 100001 corresponds to UCSC BED interval `[100000,100001)`. Illumina [TOP/BOT](../docs/glossary.md#top-bot) is a [probe](../docs/glossary.md#probe) convention, not automatically the reference forward strand; see [2.5](module_02_files_and_formats.Rmd#step-2-5). [Compression](../docs/glossary.md#compression) reduces file size. An index accelerates access but must match the exact sorted file. Renaming `.gz` does not turn ordinary gzip into bgzip.

<!-- Figure placeholder. Gemini prompt: Create an accessible format journey with three independent branches. Arrays: IDAT or CEL to calling to Final Report or PLINK. Sequencing: BCL to FASTQ, POD5 to unaligned BAM or FASTQ, and PacBio HiFi to unaligned BAM. Reads from FASTQ or unaligned BAM proceed to aligned SAM/BAM/CRAM, then gVCF/VCF. Imputation: called genotypes to BGEN or dosage VCF. All three can lead to association summary statistics. Show FASTA as a reference input to alignment and calling. Use labelled arrows, shapes and text, high contrast, no invented people or numeric research findings. -->

**Vendor format documentation:** [Illumina array inputs](https://help.dragenarray.illumina.com/dragen-array-v1.2/product-guides/input-files), [scanner outputs](https://support-docs.illumina.com/ARR/iScan/Content/ARR/iScan/GeneratedFiles_fIS.htm), [TOP/BOT definition](https://www.illumina.com/documents/products/technotes/technote_topbot.pdf), [Thermo Fisher CEL descriptions](https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/GSD/brochures/axiom-analysis-suite-user-guide.pdf) and [ONT POD5](https://software-docs.nanoporetech.com/pod5/latest/).

**Specifications:** [GA4GH file specifications](https://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/), [PLINK formats](https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/2.0/formats), [BGEN 1.2](https://www.chg.ox.ac.uk/~gav/bgen_format/spec/v1.2.html), [Hail MatrixTable](https://hail.is/docs/0.2/hail.MatrixTable.html), [Hail VariantDataset](https://hail.is/docs/0.2/vds/hail.vds.VariantDataset.html), [GWAS Catalog GWAS-SSF](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/docs/summary-statistics-format/).

**References:** [FASTQ, PMID 20015970](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20015970/); [SAM/BAM, PMID 19505943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19505943/); [VCF, PMID 21653522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21653522/); [tabix, PMID 21208982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21208982/); [BGEN, DOI 10.1101/308296](https://doi.org/10.1101/308296).

### You need

Step 1.8. The invented examples are optional reading aids, separate from the classroom dataset.

### Command

No code to run. This is a reading-only step.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

You can place a file before or after calling. You can name its companion metadata files and check its coordinate convention.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Check the producer and file header. Do not identify a format from its extension alone. Do not open a binary file as if it were a spreadsheet.

</details>

### Quick check

Are a PLINK BED file and a UCSC BED file interchangeable?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. One stores binary genotype calls. The other is a text list of genomic intervals.

## 1.10 The formats you will meet most often {#step-1-10}

Reading, about 9 minutes. You can come back to it later.

### What we do

Read fields in tiny invented examples. Conversion commands below are examples to read, not instructions to run.

### Why

The files in [examples/formats](../examples/formats/) are labelled **invented example**. S1 to S4 are invented samples. S3 has unknown sex. Five two-allele SNPs have invented GRCh38-style positions on chromosomes 1, 2 and X. One genotype is missing. S1 is male and has one allele copy at these X sites. Two reads belong to the separate 60-base contig `toy1`.

A [header](../docs/glossary.md#header) describes a file before its records. [Magic bytes](../docs/glossary.md#magic-bytes) are patterns that identify some binary encodings. The supplied binary files have `.hex.txt` companions showing their first bytes.

#### FASTQ

Open [the read example](../examples/formats/invented_example_reads.fastq). Each read occupies four lines.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Identifier line | Starts with `@`, then the read name and an optional description. |
| Sequence line | The measured DNA bases. |
| Separator line | Starts with `+`. |
| Quality line | One quality character per sequence base. |

[Phred quality](../docs/glossary.md#phred-quality) describes an estimated base-error probability. In Phred+33 encoding, `I` means quality 40.

**Common mistakes**

- The quality line must have the same length as the sequence.
- Base quality describes a base call, not confidence in its genomic placement.

Alignment software takes reads and a reference, then produces alignment records.

#### FASTA and FAI

Open [the reference](../examples/formats/invented_example_reference.fasta) and [its index](../examples/formats/invented_example_reference.fasta.fai).

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| FASTA header | Starts with `>` and names the sequence, here `toy1`. |
| FASTA sequence | The bases belonging to that named sequence. |
| FAI name | The sequence identifier. |
| FAI length | Number of bases in the sequence. |
| FAI offset | Byte position of the first sequence base, counting from zero. |
| FAI line bases | Number of sequence bases per full line. |
| FAI line width | Bytes per full line, including newline characters. |

**Common mistakes**

- Changing FASTA line breaks can invalidate its byte offsets.
- A reference name alone does not prove that two sequences match.

#### SAM, BAM, CRAM and unaligned BAM

Read [the SAM example](../examples/formats/invented_example_alignments.sam). BAM stores the same logical fields in binary. CRAM compresses read records, often against a reference. [uBAM](../docs/glossary.md#ubam) stores reads before genomic alignment.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `@HD` | Header line giving the format version and declared sort order. |
| `@SQ` | Header line naming a reference sequence and its length. |
| `@CO` | Header comment. |
| `QNAME` | Read name. |
| `FLAG` | [Bit flags](../docs/glossary.md#bit-flag) combining alignment properties. |
| `RNAME` | Reference name, or `*` without a placement. |
| `POS` | One-based alignment start, or zero without a placement. |
| `MAPQ` | Mapping quality, distinct from individual base qualities. |
| `CIGAR` | Operations describing how read and reference bases align. |
| `RNEXT` | Mate reference name; `*` when unavailable. |
| `PNEXT` | Mate position; zero when unavailable. |
| `TLEN` | Template length; zero when unavailable. |
| `SEQ` | Read bases. |
| `QUAL` | Encoded base qualities. |
| Optional tags | Extra fields written as `TAG:TYPE:VALUE`. |

The example reads are unpaired. FLAG zero means an unpaired forward alignment with no flags set. A [CIGAR](../docs/glossary.md#cigar) of `4M1I5M` describes four aligned bases, one inserted read base, then five aligned bases.

**Common mistakes**

- A BAM file can be unaligned. Its extension does not prove genomic placement.
- CIGAR `M` does not distinguish a matching base from a mismatch.
- CRAM may need the exact reference used to encode it. Its index must match the current file.

<details><summary>Example syntax, do not run</summary>

```sh
samtools view -b -o reads.bam invented_example_alignments.sam
samtools sort -o sorted.bam reads.bam
samtools index sorted.bam
```

`view -b` writes BAM. `-o` names the output. `sort` orders records by coordinate. `index` creates the region index. These operations do not call variants.

</details>

#### VCF and gVCF

Read [the multi-sample VCF](../examples/formats/invented_example_multisample.vcf), [gVCF](../examples/formats/invented_example_sample.g.vcf) and [dosage VCF](../examples/formats/invented_example_dosages.vcf). Lines beginning with `##` declare metadata. A single-hash header names the columns.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `CHROM` | Chromosome or contig name. |
| `POS` | One-based position of the first reference base. |
| `ID` | Variant identifier. |
| `REF` | Reference allele. |
| `ALT` | Alternative allele or alleles. |
| `QUAL` | Variant quality. |
| `FILTER` | Filter status; `PASS` means no listed filter failed. |
| `INFO` | Site annotations declared in the header. |
| `FORMAT` | Names and order of fields in each sample column. |
| Sample columns | Values for that sample, following `FORMAT`. |
| `GT` | [Allele indices](../docs/glossary.md#vcf-genotype): zero is REF and one is the first ALT. |
| `DS` | [Dosage](../docs/glossary.md#dosage), the expected ALT count. |
| `GP` | [Genotype probabilities](../docs/glossary.md#genotype-probability). |
| `R2` | An imputation-quality annotation whose definition depends on its producer. |
| `END` | Last included position of a gVCF reference block. |

A dot marks missing information. `0/1` means REF/first ALT; `./.` is missing. A slash leaves allele order unknown. A vertical bar records [phase](../docs/glossary.md#phasing), the arrangement across chromosome copies. A gVCF reference block uses `<NON_REF>` and `END` to represent a non-variant stretch.

For diploid calls, GP lists `0/0,0/1,1/1`. Then `DS = GP(0/1) + 2 * GP(1/1)`. For S1 on X, GP lists `0,1` and DS equals GP(1).

**Common mistakes**

- `PASS` does not prove a correct genotype.
- REF/ALT order must agree with the stated genome build.
- Rounding dosage discards uncertainty. A dosage of one need not be a certain heterozygote.

<details><summary>Example syntax, do not run</summary>

```sh
plink2 --vcf invented_example_multisample.vcf --double-id --update-sex invented_example_plink2.psam --make-pgen --out converted
```

`--vcf` selects the input. `--double-id` sets both PLINK identifiers from each sample name. `--update-sex` reads sex metadata. `--make-pgen` creates the native trio. `--out` sets its prefix. To import DS instead of calls, `--vcf` additionally needs the documented `dosage=DS` modifier.

</details>

#### Illumina Final Report, IDAT and GTC

Open [the Final Report](../examples/formats/invented_example_final_report.txt). IDAT holds earlier scanner intensities. GTC holds binary calls and related measurements. [DRAGEN Array](https://help.dragenarray.illumina.com/overview/our-features) can convert GTC to VCF.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `[Header]` | Introduces file information. |
| `[Data]` | Introduces the measurement table. |
| `SNP Name` | Array marker identifier. |
| `Sample ID` | Sample identifier. |
| `Allele1 - Forward` | First called allele on the declared forward strand. |
| `Allele2 - Forward` | Second called allele on that strand. |
| `GC Score` | Calling confidence. |
| `X` | First illustrative normalised intensity. |
| `Y` | Second illustrative normalised intensity. |

**Common mistakes**

- GC Score is not a disease probability.
- Actual exports can select different columns. Check the header before importing.
- Missing calls use `-` here. Strand labels need the matching manifest and the checks at [2.5](module_02_files_and_formats.Rmd#step-2-5).

Conversion to analysis files depends on the selected export columns and manifest.

#### PLINK 1 text and binary sets

Inspect [PED](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1.ped), [MAP](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1.map), [TPED](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1_transposed.tped), [TFAM](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1_transposed.tfam), [BIM](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1.bim) and [FAM](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1.fam). The binary [PLINK BED](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink1.bed) stores calls. Compare it with [UCSC BED](../examples/formats/invented_example_intervals.bed), a text interval file: the shared extension is a classic source of confusion.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| FID | Family identifier in FAM, TFAM and PED. |
| IID | Individual identifier in those files. |
| Father ID | Father identifier; zero means unknown. |
| Mother ID | Mother identifier; zero means unknown. |
| Sex | In FAM/TFAM/PED: 1 male, 2 female, 0 unknown. |
| Phenotype | Recorded outcome; `-9` means missing in this example. |
| Allele pairs | Two alleles per variant in PED, or per sample in TPED; `0 0` means missing. |
| Chromosome | First variant field in MAP, TPED and BIM. |
| Variant ID | Second variant field. |
| Genetic distance | Distance in [centimorgans](../docs/glossary.md#centimorgan), units based on inherited chromosome exchanges. Zero when no genetic map is supplied. |
| Base-pair position | Fourth variant field, counting from one. |
| A1 and A2 | Two extra BIM fields naming the stored alleles. |
| BED bytes | Packed calls; this variant-major file starts `6c 1b 01`. |

**Common mistakes**

- Keep each companion set together and preserve its sample and variant order.
- PLINK 1.9 often uses A1/A2 as minor/major labels. Those describe sample frequencies, not genomic REF/ALT.
- A PLINK BED cannot be read as a UCSC interval table.

<details><summary>Example syntax, do not run</summary>

```sh
plink2 --bfile invented_example_plink1 --make-pgen --out converted
```

`--bfile` reads the BED/BIM/FAM prefix. `--make-pgen` creates PGEN/PVAR/PSAM. `--out` sets the new prefix.

</details>

#### PLINK 2 native sets

Read [PVAR](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink2.pvar) and [PSAM](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink2.psam) alongside [PGEN](../examples/formats/invented_example_plink2.pgen).

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| PVAR `CHROM` | Chromosome. |
| PVAR `POS` | One-based position. |
| PVAR `ID` | Variant identifier. |
| PVAR `REF` | Reference allele. |
| PVAR `ALT` | Alternative allele. |
| PVAR `FILTER` | Optional filter status, included in this example. |
| PSAM `FID` | Family identifier. |
| PSAM `IID` | Individual identifier. |
| PSAM `SEX` | Sex code; `NA` means unknown here. |
| PGEN bytes | Genotypes and optionally dosages; starts `6c 1b`, then storage-mode information. |

**Common mistakes**

- A reference allele imported from BIM can remain provisional. Conversion does not check it against GRCh38.
- Column names matter. Read the PVAR and PSAM headers rather than assuming an order.

#### BGEN

Inspect [the BGEN bytes](../examples/formats/invented_example.bgen.hex.txt) and [sample table](../examples/formats/invented_example.sample). This BGEN 1.2 example encodes the supplied calls as certainty, with eight bits per probability.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Binary header | Variant/sample counts and encoding flags. |
| `bgen` signature | Format marker at byte offset 16. |
| Variant records | Variant identifiers, chromosome, position and alleles. |
| Probability data | Encoded genotype probabilities and chromosome-copy counts. |
| `ID_1`, `ID_2` | The two identifiers in the sample table. |
| `missing` | Fraction of missing calls in this export. |
| `sex` | Sex code; `NA` is unknown here. |
| Sample type row | Second row declaring column types. |
| `.bgi` companion | Index used to retrieve variants from the matching BGEN. |

**Common mistakes**

- Do not assume allele order. Declare the order documented by the producer.
- BGEN layout and probability precision affect decoding. Use [the specification](https://www.chg.ox.ac.uk/~gav/bgen_format/spec/v1.2.html).
- An index must match the BGEN file it describes.

<details><summary>Example syntax, do not run</summary>

```sh
plink2 --bgen invented_example.bgen ref-first --sample invented_example.sample --make-pgen --out converted
```

`--bgen` selects the file. `ref-first` declares that its first allele is reference. `--sample` supplies sample descriptions. `--make-pgen` and `--out` select the output trio and prefix.

</details>

#### Summary statistics

Open [the summary table](../examples/formats/invented_example_summary_statistics.tsv). Its effects and uncertainties are invented. Step 6.8 creates the classroom table.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `chromosome` | Chromosome label. |
| `base_pair_location` | One-based position. |
| `variant_id` | Variant identifier. |
| `effect_allele` | [Allele whose effect is reported](../docs/glossary.md#effect-allele). |
| `other_allele` | The other allele. |
| `effect_allele_frequency` | [Fraction of called alleles](../docs/glossary.md#allele-frequency) matching the effect allele. |
| `odds_ratio` | Effect on disease [odds](../docs/glossary.md#odds), the probability of disease divided by the probability of no disease. |
| `beta` | [Natural logarithm](../docs/glossary.md#logarithm) of the odds ratio. |
| `standard_error` | [Uncertainty of beta](../docs/glossary.md#standard-error) on its log-odds scale. |
| `p_value` | Evidence against the tested [null model](../docs/glossary.md#null-hypothesis) of no association. |
| `n` | Number of samples with a called genotype in this example. |

**Common mistakes**

- Read beta with its effect allele, scale and genome build.
- A missing effect is not zero.
- [GWAS-SSF](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/docs/summary-statistics-format/) submissions also need defined study metadata.

**References:** [FASTQ, PMID 20015970](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20015970/); [SAM/BAM, PMID 19505943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19505943/); [CRAM, PMID 21245279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21245279/); [CRAM 3.1, PMID 34999766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34999766/); [VCF, PMID 21653522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21653522/); [GATK, PMID 20644199](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20644199/); [PLINK, PMID 17701901](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17701901/); [second-generation PLINK, PMID 25722852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25722852/); [SAMtools/BCFtools, PMID 33590861](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33590861/); [BGEN, DOI 10.1101/308296](https://doi.org/10.1101/308296).

### You need

Step 1.9 and the linked invented examples. No classroom data or password is needed.

### Command

No code to run. This is a reading-only step. The shell examples in Why show conversion syntax only.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

You can explain the header and fields of each example. The genotype files describe five variants, four samples and one missing genotype.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

A binary file will not look like a readable table. Use its JSON description and hex dump. The illustrative conversion outputs are not needed for any later step.

</details>

### Quick check

An imputed sample has probabilities `0.1, 0.8, 0.1`. What is its ALT dosage, and is that a certain heterozygous call?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The dosage is `0.8 + 2 * 0.1 = 1`. It is not certainty: the two homozygous possibilities still have probability 0.1 each.

</details>

### Files created

None. The supplied examples are separate reading aids.

## 1.11 How large projects share genetic data {#step-1-11}

Reading, about 3 minutes. You can come back to it later.

### What we do

Compare three controlled-access resources. [Controlled access](../docs/glossary.md#controlled-access) means that approved researchers use data under specified permissions.

### Why

[UK Biobank](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/15468170680605-Genome-wide-genotyping) combines array calls with imputation and sequencing. Its arrays were UK BiLEVE Axiom and UK Biobank Axiom, now associated with Thermo Fisher. Called array data can use PLINK sets. Imputed genotypes use BGEN probabilities with sample descriptions.

The [initial DRAGEN whole-genome release](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/26272701015837-Initial-DRAGEN-whole-genome-sequencing-WGS-data-release) has about 1.2 [PB](../docs/glossary.md#storage-units) of pVCF. A [pVCF](../docs/glossary.md#pvcf) is a project-level VCF containing calls across many samples. One petabyte (PB) is 1,000 terabytes (TB) in decimal units. The release uses [machine learning](../docs/glossary.md#machine-learning), a model fitted to patterns in data, to help identify poor calls. The [corrected release documentation](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/26273057297949-ML-Corrected-DRAGEN-whole-genome-sequencing-WGS-release) reports about 5.5 TB for the per-chromosome PGEN/PVAR/PSAM sets. These retain information equivalent to the **biallelic reduced pVCF**, which represents [two-allele sites](../docs/glossary.md#biallelic-multiallelic) with reduced fields. They do not retain every field of the initial [multiallelic](../docs/glossary.md#biallelic-multiallelic) pVCF, which can list more than one alternative allele. The comparison illustrates both compact encoding and selection of information for analysis.

[All of Us](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/methods/) offers array and sequencing data in its research environment. Array exports include VCF, PLINK and Hail MatrixTable representations. Short-read whole-genome data include CRAM and Hail VariantDataset. The [VariantDataset documentation](https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/14927774297620-The-new-VariantDataset-VDS-format-for-All-of-Us-short-read-WGS-data) estimates well over 50 TB for 250,000 genomes as VCF. This estimate explains the switch to a Hail VariantDataset for the complete set. It keeps reference blocks and avoids a full sample-by-variant table. Smaller selected sets remain available as VCF, PLINK or MatrixTable. An exome subset selected from whole-genome sequencing is not a separate whole-exome experiment.

[dbGaP](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gap/) is a controlled-access archive across studies. Its [submission guide](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gap/docs/moleculardatasection/) prefers PLINK sets for array data, with raw Illumina IDAT or Affymetrix CEL files when available. It requests PLINK rather than VCF for chip data. Sequence variants and linked reads follow their own submission requirements. Sequence reads and alignments may be linked through the Sequence Read Archive, an archive for sequencing measurements. Read each study's file descriptions and access conditions.

Why offer more than one representation? A [distributed dataset](../docs/glossary.md#distributed-data) can spread work across many computers. Hail stores make repeated cohort-wide processing practical. BGEN keeps probability information compact. PLINK sets support efficient association tools. CRAM retains read-level evidence. Summary statistics are smaller but cannot answer every question about individual calls. Format choice is about scale, retained information and intended analysis, not which extension is newest.

**References:** [UK Biobank, PMID 30305743](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30305743/); [All of Us genomic data, PMID 38374255](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38374255/); [dbGaP, PMID 24297256](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24297256/).

## Module 1 recap {#module-1-recap}

- You separated a variant, an allele and a genotype.
- You saw that the array measures light, and that a calling algorithm turns it into genotypes.
- The annotation lists 299,523 array entries on chromosomes 1 to 22, X, Y and MT.
- The laboratory ran 21 plates of 96 wells, which gives 2,016 measurements; 16 wells are technical replicates of the 2,000 simulated people.
- You checked that the genotype files hold 2,016 samples and 299,523 variants, with no QC applied and no person removed.

- You compared arrays, sequencing and imputation, then read invented format examples.
- You saw why large resources share several representations of the same study.
